questions.question: Which Indian state hosts the world's largest floating solar power plant, operational since 2023?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Madhya Pradesh**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• **Madhya Pradesh** is home to the **world's largest floating solar power plant**, which became operational in **2023**. 
 
• The solar power plant is located at the **Omkareshwar Dam reservoir** on the Narmada River in Khandwa district, Madhya Pradesh. 
 
• It has a total capacity of **600 MW**, making it the largest floating solar project globally. 
 
• The project aims to increase the use of **renewable energy** in India and reduce dependence on fossil fuels. 
 
• This plant is expected to help Madhya Pradesh meet its **renewable energy targets** and contribute significantly to India's clean energy initiatives. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 
 
• **Floating Solar Power Plants:** 
 
 
• Floating solar power plants are built on water bodies like reservoirs, lakes, and dams, utilizing unused water surfaces. 
 
• These plants help conserve land, which is particularly beneficial in densely populated areas. 
 
• They also reduce water evaporation, helping conserve water in reservoirs. 
 
• Floating solar panels operate more efficiently due to the cooling effect of water. 
 
 
 
• **Omkareshwar Dam:** 
 
 
• The Omkareshwar Dam is located on the **Narmada River** and is a key infrastructure supporting agriculture and electricity generation. 
 
• The reservoir created by the dam is now being utilized for the floating solar project. 
 
 
 
• **Renewable Energy in India:** 
 
 
• India is aggressively working to achieve its renewable energy target of **500 GW** by 2030 under the Paris Agreement. 
 
• Solar energy is a significant contributor, with India ranking among the leading nations in solar power capacity globally. 
 
• The floating solar plant in Madhya Pradesh is part of this larger effort to transition toward sustainable energy. 
 
 
 
• **Global Context:** 
 
 
• Floating solar plants are becoming popular globally in countries like **China, Japan, and South Korea** due to their land conservation benefits. 
 
• India's Omkareshwar project sets a global benchmark in capacity and technology. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
 
• **Advantages of Floating Solar Plants:** 
 
 
• Efficient land usage: No need for vast land areas like traditional solar farms. 
 
• Reduced water evaporation: The panels protect the water surface from sunlight exposure. 
 
• Improved efficiency: Panels remain cooler, enhancing energy generation. 
 
• Eco-friendly: Helps reduce carbon emissions and promotes clean energy. 
 
 
 
• **Madhya Pradesh's Renewable Energy Goals:** 
 
 
• The state aims to become a renewable energy hub, focusing on solar, wind, and hydropower. 
 
• The floating solar plant aligns with India's larger commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by **2070**.

questions.question: Which of the following is classified as a galaxy?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Andromeda**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Andromeda** is a spiral galaxy located approximately **2.537 million light-years** from Earth. It is the closest large galaxy to the Milky Way.
 
• It is also known as **M31**, Messier 31, or NGC 224, and is part of the Local Group of galaxies, which includes the Milky Way, Triangulum, and around 54 other smaller galaxies.
 
• The Andromeda Galaxy is massive, containing approximately **one trillion stars**, which is more than twice the number of stars in the Milky Way.
 
• It is visible to the naked eye from Earth in areas with dark skies and is often studied to understand galaxy formation, structure, and dynamics.
 
• Unlike stars, constellations, or star systems, galaxies like Andromeda are vast collections of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter bound together by gravity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sirius:**

 
 
• Sirius, also known as the **Dog Star**, is the brightest star in the night sky. It is located in the constellation Canis Major.
 
• Sirius is a binary star system consisting of Sirius A and its faint companion, Sirius B.
 
• It is approximately **8.6 light-years** away from Earth, making it one of the closest stars to our planet.
 
• Sirius is not a galaxy but a star system.
 
 
 
• **Orion:**
 
 
• Orion is a prominent constellation visible from Earth, famous for the **Orion Belt**, which consists of three aligned stars.
 
• It contains notable stars like **Betelgeuse** and **Rigel**, and features the Orion Nebula, which is a stellar nursery.
 
• Orion is not a galaxy but a group of stars forming a recognizable pattern.
 
 
 
• **Ursa Minor:**
 
 
• Ursa Minor, or the **Little Bear**, is a constellation known for containing the **North Star** (Polaris), which is a key navigational star.
 
• It is located near the celestial north pole and is used to find direction in the Northern Hemisphere.
 
• Ursa Minor is not a galaxy but a constellation.
 
 
 
• **Galaxies:**
 
 
• A galaxy is a massive system consisting of stars, stellar remnants, interstellar gas, dust, and dark matter bound together by gravity.
 
• The Milky Way (our galaxy), Andromeda, and Triangulum are part of the Local Group of galaxies.
 
• Galaxies come in different types, such as **spiral, elliptical, and irregular**, each with unique characteristics and structures.
 
• Galaxies are studied to understand cosmic phenomena like star formation, black holes, and dark matter.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Andromeda-Milky Way Collision:**

 
 
• The Andromeda Galaxy is on a collision course with the Milky Way, predicted to occur in approximately **4.5 billion years**.
 
• This event will result in the formation of a new galaxy, sometimes referred to as **Milkomeda**.
 
 
 
• **Galactic Research:**
 
 
• Studying galaxies like Andromeda helps scientists understand cosmic evolution, including the formation and lifecycle of stars.
 
• Research on galaxies contributes to insights into phenomena such as **supermassive black holes** and the distribution of **dark matter**.
 
 
 
• **Messier Objects:**
 
 
• Andromeda is part of the **Messier catalog**, which lists astronomical objects like galaxies, nebulae, and star clusters.
 
• These objects are frequently studied by astronomers due to their accessibility and scientific importance.

questions.question: What happens during the process of transcription in cells?

options.text: DNA is replicated into identical copies
Proteins are folded into functional shapes

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**DNA is converted into RNA**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Transcription** is the biological process where the **DNA sequence of a gene is copied into RNA**. It is the first step in gene expression.
 
• The enzyme **RNA polymerase** plays a central role in this process by binding to the DNA at the promoter region and synthesizing a complementary strand of RNA.
 
• In transcription, the DNA strand used as a template is called the **template strand**, while the complementary strand is referred to as the **coding strand**.
 
• The result of transcription is a single-stranded RNA molecule that is complementary to the DNA template strand. This RNA can be **messenger RNA (mRNA)**, **ribosomal RNA (rRNA)**, or **transfer RNA (tRNA)**, depending on the gene being transcribed.
 
• Transcription occurs in the nucleus

questions.question: What is the difference between displacement and distance?

options.text: Distance includes direction; displacement does not
Displacement includes direction; distance does not

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Displacement includes direction; distance does not**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__
 
__ 

• **Displacement** is a vector quantity that specifies the shortest straight-line distance between the initial and final positions of an object, along with the direction of movement. 

• **Distance**, on the other hand, is a scalar quantity that measures the total length of the path traveled by an object, irrespective of the direction. 

• Displacement can have a positive, negative, or zero value depending on the direction of motion, while distance is always positive and cannot be negative. 

• For example, if an object moves 10 meters forward and then 10 meters backward to its starting point, the displacement is 0 meters (due to no net change in position), while the distance is 20 meters. 

• Displacement considers direction and magnitude, making it more specific for indicating the change in position, whereas distance only measures magnitude, making it less specific. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Vector Quantity:** 

• A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Examples include displacement, velocity, acceleration, and force. 

• Displacement is a vector quantity because it specifies both the magnitude (shortest distance) and direction. 
 
 

• **Scalar Quantity:** 

• A scalar quantity has only magnitude and no direction. Examples include distance, speed, mass, and temperature. 

• Distance is a scalar quantity because it measures only the magnitude of the path traveled. 
 
 

• **Applications:** 

• Displacement is used in physics for calculations involving motion, such as determining velocity and acceleration. 

• Distance is commonly used for practical purposes like measuring travel lengths or determining road routes. 
 
 

• **Example:** 

• If a person walks 3 km north and then 4 km east, the distance traveled is 7 km, while the displacement (using Pythagoras theorem) is 5 km northeast. 

• This highlights the difference between the total path traveled (distance) and the shortest path between two points (displacement). 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Directional Significance:** Displacement’s inclusion of direction makes it crucial for vector-based calculations in physics, while distance is used for scalar measurements. 

• **Zero Displacement:** If an object returns to its starting point after movement, displacement is zero, but distance measures the total path traveled. 

• **Real-Life Scenarios:** Distance is practical for everyday usage (e.g., driving or running), while displacement is essential for scientific experiments and modeling motion. 

• **Geographical Representation:** In maps, displacement is represented as straight-line distance between two points, while distance considers the curved or actual traveled path.

questions.question: What is the main goal of the Ayushman Bharat scheme?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To provide affordable healthcare**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
 
 
• **Ayushman Bharat**, also known as the **Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PMJAY)**, was launched by the Government of India to provide **accessible and affordable healthcare services** to economically weaker sections of society. 
 
• The scheme aims to **cover over 10 crore poor and vulnerable families**, offering a coverage of up to **Rs. 5 lakh per family per year** for secondary and tertiary hospitalization. 
 
• Ayushman Bharat focuses on two main components: **Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs)** and the **PMJAY health insurance scheme**. HWCs aim to provide **comprehensive primary healthcare services**, while PMJAY ensures **financial protection for hospitalization costs**. 
 
• The scheme is designed to reduce **out-of-pocket healthcare expenses**, ensuring that families below the poverty line receive **cashless treatment** at empanelled public and private hospitals.

questions.question: Medha Patkar led a movement to protest against a large dam's construction? What was the name of the movement?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Narmada Bachao Andolan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Medha Patkar** is a prominent Indian social activist who led the **Narmada Bachao Andolan (NBA)**, a movement protesting the construction of large dams on the **Narmada River**, including the Sardar Sarovar Dam.
 
• The **Narmada Bachao Andolan** (Save the Narmada Movement) began in **1985** and primarily opposed the displacement of local communities and environmental damage caused by the dam's construction.
 
• The primary concern of the movement was the displacement of thousands of **tribal people, farmers, and villagers** whose homes and lands were submerged due to the dam projects.
 
• The NBA also highlighted the lack of proper **rehabilitation and resettlement** policies for the affected people and raised concerns about the ecological impact, including deforestation and loss of biodiversity.
 
• The movement gained international attention and raised significant debates on the costs and benefits of large-scale development projects, questioning their impact on marginalized communities.
 
• Despite its opposition, the **Sardar Sarovar Dam** was completed, but the NBA succeeded in bringing attention to the plight of displaced people and the importance of sustainable development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Medha Patkar:**

 
 
• Medha Patkar, born on **1 December 1954**, is a renowned social reformer and environmental activist.
 
• She founded the **Narmada Bachao Andolan** and has worked extensively for the rights of displaced people, particularly in tribal and rural areas.
 
• Her activism has also extended to other issues, including urban slum redevelopment and women’s rights.
 
• She has received several awards, including the **Right Livelihood Award** in 1991 for her efforts in environmental and social justice.
 
 
 
• **Sardar Sarovar Dam:**
 
 
• The **Sardar Sarovar Dam** is a major dam on the **Narmada River** in Gujarat, India.
 
• It is part of the Narmada Valley Project, which includes the construction of several dams and canals aimed at providing **irrigation, drinking water, and hydroelectric power**.
 
• The dam is one of the largest infrastructure projects in India and has been a subject of both praise and criticism due to its economic benefits and social/environmental costs.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Concerns:**
 
 
• Large dams like the Sardar Sarovar cause significant environmental impacts, including **deforestation, loss of wildlife habitats, and changes to river ecosystems**.
 
• Such projects also lead to the submersion of fertile agricultural lands and displacement of local communities.
 
 
 
• **Other Movements Led by Medha Patkar:**
 
 
• She has also been part of the **Right to Information (RTI) movement** and the **National Alliance of People's Movements (NAPM)**, which advocates for various social justice causes.
 
• Patkar has been vocal about issues related to urban displacement, particularly in Mumbai, where she campaigned against the demolition of slums.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Chipko Movement:**

 
 
• The **Chipko Movement**, initiated in the 1970s in Uttarakhand (then part of Uttar Pradesh), was an environmental movement to **protect trees and forests** from being cut down.
 
• It involved villagers, particularly women, hugging trees to prevent their felling, hence the name "Chipko" (meaning "to hug").
 
 
 
• **Save Ganga Movement:**
 
 
• This movement focuses on cleaning and conserving the **Ganga River**, which is considered sacred in India but is heavily polluted.
 
• Initiatives under this movement include the **Namami Gange Programme**, launched by the Indian government to rejuvenate the river.
 
 
 
• **Project Tiger:**
 
 
• Launched in **1973**, this project aims to conserve the tiger population in India and its natural habitats.
 
• It has led to the establishment of several **tiger reserves** across the country.

questions.question: Which of the following is not one of the domains measured by the Happiness Index?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Internet speed**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Happiness Index** is a global measure used to evaluate the happiness and well-being of individuals in various countries.
 
• The index typically considers several domains that contribute to happiness, such as **health, psychological well-being, education, environment, and social relationships**.
 
• **Internet speed** is not a domain included in the Happiness Index. While technology and connectivity are important, they are not directly measured as part of the Happiness Index.
 
• Domains like **health** focus on physical and mental well-being, while **psychological well-being** evaluates emotional states such as contentment and stress levels.
 
• The **environment** domain assesses factors such as air quality, access to green spaces, and sustainable practices, which have a direct impact on people's happiness.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Happiness Index:**
 
 
• The Happiness Index is often derived from surveys like the **World Happiness Report**, which ranks countries based on factors like GDP per capita, social support, life expectancy, and freedom.
 
• It is widely used by governments and organizations to assess societal well-being and identify areas of improvement.
 
 
 
• **Health as a domain:**
 
 
• Health plays a crucial role in happiness, as physical and mental well-being significantly impact life satisfaction.
 
• Countries with better healthcare systems and higher life expectancy often score higher on the Happiness Index.
 
 
 
• **Environment as a domain:**
 
 
• A clean and sustainable environment contributes to happiness by reducing stress and enhancing quality of life.
 
• Countries with better air and water quality and access to green spaces tend to rank higher in environmental factors.
 
 
 
• **Psychological well-being:**
 
 
• This domain evaluates emotional and mental health, including levels of stress, anxiety, and overall contentment.
 
• Policies promoting mental health care and emotional support systems are vital for improving psychological well-being.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Internet speed:**
 
 
• While internet speed is essential for connectivity and technological advancement, it is not a direct factor in measuring happiness.
 
• However, better internet speed can indirectly affect happiness by improving access to education, communication, and entertainment.
 
 
 
• **Global Rankings:**
 
 
• Countries like **Finland, Denmark, and Switzerland** consistently rank high in the Happiness Index due to their focus on health, environment, and social support.
 
• Efforts to improve the Happiness Index often involve policies targeting education, healthcare, and environmental sustainability.

questions.question: Under which article of the Indian Constitution is the Right to Equality guaranteed?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 14 to Article 18**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Right to Equality** is guaranteed under **Articles 14 to 18** of the Indian Constitution. It is one of the fundamental rights provided to citizens of India.
 
• **Article 14:** Guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. This ensures no discrimination against individuals on any grounds.
 
• **Article 15:** Prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. It also enables the state to make special provisions for women, children, and socially disadvantaged groups.
 
• **Article 16:** Ensures equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. It prohibits discrimination in employment based on religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, or residence.
 
• **Article 17:** Abolishes "untouchability" and forbids its practice in any form. This article is a step towards eradicating caste-based discrimination in society.
 
• **Article 18:** Abolishes titles except for military and academic distinctions. It aims to prevent the creation of artificial hierarchies in Indian society.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution, providing citizens with basic human rights essential for their development.
 
• These rights are enforceable by the courts, ensuring protection against arbitrary actions by the state.
 
• They include the Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
 
 
• **Article 14:**
 
 
• It emphasizes equality before the law, ensuring that every individual is subject to the same laws without favoritism.
 
• The concept of "equal protection of the laws" guarantees that individuals in similar circumstances will be treated equally.
 
 
 
• **Article 15:**
 
 
• It prohibits discrimination on specific grounds, fostering inclusivity and social justice.
 
• The state is empowered to make affirmative actions like reservations for disadvantaged groups.
 
 
 
• **Article 17:**
 
 
• This article is instrumental in abolishing untouchability, a social evil prevalent in India.
 
• It ensures that individuals belonging to the lower castes are treated equally and with dignity.
 
 
 
• **Article 18:**
 
 
• It prevents individuals from using titles that create social hierarchies, ensuring a classless society.
 
• Military and academic distinctions are exceptions under this article.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights vs Directive Principles:**

 
 
• Fundamental Rights are enforceable by courts, while Directive Principles of State Policy are non-enforceable guidelines for governance.
 
• Both aim to establish a welfare state but differ in their legal binding nature.
 
 
 
• **Equality vs Equity:**
 
 
• Equality ensures equal treatment for all, while equity focuses on fairness and addressing disparities.
 
• Articles 15 and 16 incorporate elements of equity through affirmative actions like reservations.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Interpretation:**
 
 
• The judiciary plays a crucial role in interpreting and safeguarding fundamental rights.
 
• Landmark cases like Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala reaffirm the importance of fundamental rights in India's constitutional framework.

questions.question: What does the term 'aggregate demand' refer to in macroeconomics?

options.text: Total demand for a specific product
Total demand for goods and services in an economy

questions.solution: The correct answer is __**Total demand for goods and services in an economy**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** • **Aggregate demand** refers to the **total quantity of goods and services** demanded across all sectors of an economy at a given overall price level and within a specific time period. • It is represented as the **sum of consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports (exports minus imports)**. The formula is often expressed as: **AD = C + I + G + (X - M)**. • Aggregate demand encompasses the demand for all products and services in an economy, not just a specific product or service. • It plays a **crucial role in determining the overall economic activity** since higher aggregate demand leads to increased production, employment, and income levels. • The concept is a central component of **Keynesian economics**, which emphasizes the importance of demand-side management for achieving economic stability and growth.

questions.question: Who acts as the chairperson during a joint meeting of both houses of Parliament?
questions.solution: The correct answer is __**Lok Sabha Speaker**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** • The **Lok Sabha Speaker** presides over the joint sitting of both houses of Parliament as per **Article 118** of the Indian Constitution. • A joint sitting is convened in case of a deadlock between the **Lok Sabha** and **Rajya Sabha** on specific bills. It is a method to resolve disagreements between the two houses. • The Lok Sabha Speaker holds this position as the presiding officer of the lower house and is responsible for maintaining order during the session. • If the Lok Sabha Speaker is absent, the **Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha** presides over the meeting. If both are unavailable, the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha may preside. • The joint sitting provision is applicable only for **ordinary bills** and not for **constitutional amendment bills**. It is mentioned under **Article 108** of the Constitution.

questions.question: Which key goal does the Swachh Bharat Mission focus on?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sanitation and hygiene**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• **Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM)** was launched by **Prime Minister Narendra Modi** on **2nd October 2014**, marking the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi. 
 
• The mission primarily aims to achieve universal access to **sanitation facilities** and eliminate open defecation in India by constructing individual household toilets, community toilets, and public toilets. 
 
• The campaign emphasizes **behavioral change** to promote hygiene practices, including handwashing and waste segregation at the household level. 
 
• It also focuses on creating awareness about the importance of sanitation and hygiene through **public outreach programs**, school campaigns, and media engagement. 
 
• The Swachh Bharat Mission consists of two sub-missions: **Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban)** and **Swachh Bharat Mission (Gramin)**, addressing urban and rural sanitation challenges respectively. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Objective of Swachh Bharat Mission:** 
 
 
• The mission aims to achieve a **clean and open defecation-free India** by **2nd October 2019**, coinciding with the 150th birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi. 
 
• Promote the use of bio-toilets, solid waste management, and proper drainage systems to ensure better sanitation infrastructure. 
 
• Encourage active participation from **government bodies, private sectors, NGOs, and citizens** in maintaining cleanliness. 
 
 
 
• **Funding Mechanism:** 
 
 
• The Swachh Bharat Mission is funded through allocations from the **central government, state governments, and private partnerships**. 
 
• The **Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)** contributions also play a significant role in funding sanitation-related projects. 
 
 
 
• **Achievements:** 
 
 
• As of **2023**, India has successfully constructed more than **11 crore toilets** under the Swachh Bharat Mission. 
 
• Over **600,000 villages** have been declared open defecation-free (ODF), contributing to improved public health and hygiene. 
 
 
 
• **Impact on Public Health:** 
 
 
• Reduction in diseases such as **diarrhea, cholera, and typhoid** due to improved sanitation facilities. 
 
• Enhanced quality of life in rural and urban areas through better waste management and hygiene practices. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Key Features:** 
 
 
• **Urban Component:** Focuses on waste management, sewer networks, and public toilets in cities and towns. 
 
• **Rural Component:** Targets the construction of individual household latrines and awareness campaigns in villages. 
 
• **Behavioral Change:** Encourages citizens to adopt hygiene practices such as handwashing and proper waste disposal. 
 
 
 
• **Related Government Programs:** 
 
 
• **National Rural Health Mission (NRHM):** Supports the sanitation goals of SBM by improving health outcomes in rural areas. 
 
• **Namami Gange Program:** Works alongside SBM to clean the Ganges river and promote sanitation practices in adjacent regions. 
 
• **Smart Cities Mission:** Integrates SBM goals into urban planning to ensure sustainable waste management and sanitation infrastructure.

questions.question: Which group primarily benefits from the Stand-Up India Scheme?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Women and SC/ST entrepreneurs**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• The **Stand-Up India Scheme** was launched by the **Government of India on April 5, 2016**, with the objective of promoting **entrepreneurship among women and Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST)**. 
 
• The scheme primarily provides **bank loans ranging from Rs. 10 lakh to Rs. 1 crore** to at least one Scheduled Caste (SC) or Scheduled Tribe (ST) borrower and one woman borrower per bank branch for setting up a greenfield enterprise. 
 
• The enterprise could be in the sectors of **manufacturing, services, agri-allied activities, or trading**. The main aim is to encourage economic participation from these underrepresented groups. 
 
• The scheme is implemented through all branches of **Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs)** across India, ensuring widespread accessibility. 
 
• It also provides **handholding support** by facilitating guidance, mentorship, and assistance with registration and other requirements. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Eligibility Criteria:** 
 
 
• The applicant must be a **woman or belong to the SC/ST category**. 
 
• The age of the borrower must be **above 18 years**. 
 
• The loans are specifically for **greenfield projects**, i.e., the first-time venture of the beneficiary in manufacturing, services, or trading sectors. 
 
• The borrower should not be in default to any bank or financial institution. 
 
 

 
• **Loan Details:** 
 
 
• The loan amount ranges from **Rs. 10 lakh to Rs. 1 crore**. 
 
• The scheme provides a **composite loan** (inclusive of term loan and working capital) for setting up an enterprise. 
 
• The repayment period for the loan is up to **7 years**, with a maximum moratorium period of 18 months. 
 
 

 
• **Support System:** 
 
 
• The scheme includes a dedicated portal (**Stand-Up Mitra**) that offers handholding support and connects borrowers with banks and other stakeholders. 
 
• Mentorship and guidance are provided to help applicants with technical and financial expertise. 
 
 

 
• **Achievements:** 
 
 
• Since its inception in **2016**, the scheme has supported thousands of women and SC/ST entrepreneurs in setting up their businesses. 
 
• It has contributed significantly to **financial inclusion** and the empowerment of marginalized communities in India. 
 
 

 
• **Comparison with Other Schemes:** 
 
 
• Unlike schemes like **Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana**, which focuses on micro-enterprises, the Stand-Up India Scheme specifically targets women and SC/ST entrepreneurs for medium-scale businesses. 
 
• It also ensures **social equity** by addressing the economic challenges faced by these groups. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Key Data:** As of **March 2023**, more than **1.5 lakh beneficiaries** have been sanctioned loans under the Stand-Up India Scheme, with a significant proportion being women entrepreneurs. 
 
• **Sectoral Focus:** The scheme encourages innovation and entrepreneurship in sectors like **manufacturing, services, and agriculture-allied activities**, driving economic growth in rural and urban areas. 
 
• **Inclusivity:** The focus on SC/ST and women entrepreneurs highlights the government’s commitment to **social and economic empowerment** of marginalized groups in India.

questions.question: What is the term used to refer the process of people leaving their home country to settle in another?
questions.solution: The correct answer is __**Emigration**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** • **Emigration** refers to the process of people leaving their **home country** to settle permanently in another country. It is focused on the act of leaving one's native land. • The term "emigration" is derived from the Latin word **"emigrare,"** which means "to move away." • Emigration occurs due to various reasons such as **better economic opportunities, political stability, family reunification, and environmental factors**. • It is important to note that emigration is seen from the perspective of the **home country**, as opposed to immigration, which is viewed from the perspective of the **destination country**. • For example, if a person moves from **India to the United States**, India would consider it as emigration, while the United States would consider it as immigration.

questions.question: Which Indian city had the highest population as per the 2011 Census?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mumbai**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mumbai**, also known as the financial capital of India, had the highest population as per the **2011 Census**. The city's population was recorded at approximately **12.4 million** within its municipal limits.
 
• Mumbai is the largest city in Maharashtra and is ranked as the most populous city in India, surpassing cities like **Delhi**, **Kolkata**, and **Bengaluru**.
 
• The city is a major hub for industries such as finance, entertainment (Bollywood), and trade, attracting people from across the country for employment and better living opportunities.
 
• As per the **2011 Census data**, Mumbai was categorized as a **megacity** due to its extremely high population density, significant urbanization, and economic importance.
 
• While **Delhi** is the capital of India and also has a high population, Mumbai's population within its municipal boundaries surpassed Delhi's population figures.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Population of Indian Cities as per the 2011 Census:**

 
 
• **Mumbai:** Approximately **12.4 million** within the municipal limits and over **20 million** in the metropolitan region.
 
• **Delhi:** Approximately **11 million** within municipal limits and around **16.7 million** in the National Capital Territory (NCT).
 
• **Kolkata:** Recorded a population of around **4.5 million** within municipal limits, while the metropolitan area had a population of over **14 million**.
 
• **Bengaluru:** Had a population of approximately **8.4 million** within city limits as per the 2011 Census.
 
 
 
• **Urbanization in Mumbai:**
 
 
• Mumbai is one of the most urbanized regions in India, with a population density of approximately **20,482 people per square kilometer** as per the 2011 Census.
 
• The city is known for its **mixed culture**, housing people from various parts of the country, and offering a cosmopolitan lifestyle.
 
• The **Greater Mumbai region** is governed by the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), which is one of the richest municipal corporations in Asia.
 
 
 
• **Economic Importance of Mumbai:**
 
 
• Mumbai contributes significantly to India's **GDP**, accounting for over **6%** of the national economy.
 
• It houses major financial institutions, including the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, **Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE)**, and the headquarters of numerous multinational companies.
 
• The city's **Bollywood film industry** is the largest in India, generating substantial revenue and employment.
 
 
 
• **Challenges Due to Population:**
 
 
• Mumbai faces challenges such as **traffic congestion**, **housing shortages**, and **pollution** due to its high population density.
 
• The city also struggles with the proliferation of **slums**, with areas like Dharavi being one of the largest slum regions in Asia.
 
• Efforts are being made by the government to improve urban infrastructure, housing, and public transport systems to address these challenges.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **2011 Census:** Conducted by the **Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India**, the 2011 Census provided comprehensive data on India's population, including urban and rural demographics.
 
• **Megacities:** As per the Census, cities like Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, and Chennai were classified as **megacities** due to their significant population size and economic importance.
 
• **Population Growth:** Rapid urbanization has led to a steady increase in population in cities like Mumbai, driven by migration and natural growth.
 
• **Government Initiatives:** Programs such as **Smart Cities Mission** and urban development schemes aim to improve the infrastructure and living standards in cities like Mumbai.

questions.question: In which imaginary town are most of R.K. Narayan's famous works set?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Malgudi**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__
 
__ 

• **Malgudi** is an **imaginary South Indian town** created by the renowned Indian English writer **R.K. Narayan**. It served as the setting for most of his novels and short stories. 

• The town of Malgudi was first introduced in **"Swami and Friends" (1935)**, R.K. Narayan's debut novel, and continued to appear in many of his subsequent works. 

• Malgudi represents a typical small-town atmosphere in India, reflecting the culture, traditions, and lifestyle of the Indian middle class during the 20th century. 

• This fictional town is characterized by locations such as the **Sarayu River**, **Market Road**, the **Board High School**, and **Lawley Extension**, which form the backdrop for the stories. 

• R.K. Narayan's portrayal of Malgudi and its inhabitants is widely appreciated for its simplicity and relatability, making it a cornerstone of Indian English literature. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
 

• **About R.K. Narayan:** 
 

• R.K. Narayan (1906–2001) is one of India's most celebrated writers in English. His full name is **Rasipuram Krishnaswami Iyer Narayanaswami**. 

• He is known for his unique ability to capture the essence of Indian life through his simple yet profound storytelling. 

• Some of his most notable works include **"The Bachelor of Arts," "The Guide," "The English Teacher,"** and **"Malgudi Days."** 

• R.K. Narayan was awarded the **Sahitya Akademi Award** in 1960 for his novel **"The Guide,"** which was later adapted into a critically acclaimed film. 
 
 

• **Characteristics of Malgudi:** 
 

• Malgudi is a blend of **fictional and real-world elements,** making it relatable to readers while retaining its uniqueness. 

• The town is inspired by several South Indian cities, including **Mysore** and **Chennai**. 

• It contains iconic places like the **Albert Mission School, Malgudi Railway Station, Kabir Street,** and **Sarayu River,** which create a vivid setting for the stories. 

• Malgudi’s residents are ordinary people with relatable struggles, aspirations, and quirks, reflecting the socio-cultural dynamics of India. 
 
 

• **Other Locations in the Options:** 
 

• **Panchgani:** A real hill station in Maharashtra, known for its scenic beauty and boarding schools. It is not related to R.K. Narayan's works. 

• **Shimla:** A famous hill station and the capital of Himachal Pradesh, often featured in other literary works but not in R.K. Narayan's writings. 

• **Darjeeling:** A hill station in West Bengal, renowned for its tea plantations and colonial heritage, but unrelated to R.K. Narayan's fictional town. 
 
 

• **Legacy of Malgudi:** 
 

• Malgudi gained immense popularity through the **TV series "Malgudi Days,"** directed by Shankar Nag and based on R.K. Narayan’s short stories. 

• The series, featuring actor **Master Manjunath** as Swami, brought the town and its characters to life, earning a cult following. 

• Malgudi is often viewed as a metaphor for India itself, capturing the essence of its culture, struggles, and transitions over time.

questions.question: Which material was commonly used in Mathura sculptures?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Red Sandstone**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
 

• The sculptures of **Mathura**, a significant art center during ancient India, primarily utilized **red sandstone**, which was widely available in the region. 

• **Red sandstone** is characterized by its smooth texture, durability, and reddish hue, making it ideal for creating intricate sculptures and architectural elements. 

• The **Kushan period** (1st–3rd century CE) saw a flourishing of Mathura art, where red sandstone was extensively used to craft statues of **Buddha**, **Jain Tirthankaras**, and other religious figures.

questions.question: Which of the following is a classical form of Indian music?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hindustani**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Hindustani music** is one of the two principal styles of Indian classical music, the other being Carnatic music.
 
• It originated in the **northern parts of India** and has been influenced by Persian and Islamic traditions.
 
• This classical form encompasses various genres such as **Dhrupad, Khayal, Tappa, Thumri, and Tarana**, with unique features and approaches to melody and rhythm.
 
• The **foundation of Hindustani music** lies in ragas (melodic frameworks) and talas (rhythmic cycles), which define the structure and emotional expression of compositions.
 
• Prominent Hindustani musicians include **Ravi Shankar, Ustad Bismillah Khan, Ustad Zakir Hussain, and Pt. Bhimsen Joshi**, who have contributed significantly to its global recognition.

questions.question: Which color medal is awarded for the first position in the Olympics?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gold**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• **Gold medals** are awarded to athletes who achieve **first place** in their respective events at the Olympics, symbolizing the highest level of achievement in sports. 
 
• The tradition of awarding medals in the Olympics began in the **1904 Summer Olympics**, held in St. Louis, USA, where gold, silver, and bronze medals were introduced as awards. 
 
• Gold medals are made primarily of **silver** and are coated with a thin layer of pure gold. As per the **International Olympic Committee (IOC)**, the gold coating must be at least **6 grams**. 
 
• The design of the medal varies for each Olympics, showcasing unique elements of the host country’s culture and traditions. 
 
• Athletes who win a gold medal at the Olympics are often celebrated globally and receive various honors from their home countries, including monetary rewards and recognition. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 
 
• **Silver Medal:** 
 
• A silver medal is awarded to the athlete or team that secures **second place** in their event at the Olympics. 
 
• It is made primarily of **pure silver**, signifying the second-highest achievement in sports. 
 
• The tradition of silver medals dates back to the **1896 Summer Olympics**, where winners were awarded silver medals instead of gold. 
 
 
• **Bronze Medal:** 
 
• A bronze medal is awarded to the athlete or team that finishes in **third place** in their event. 
 
• It is made of a combination of **copper and tin**, representing the third tier of excellence in sports. 
 
• Bronze medals were introduced in the **1904 Olympics**, along with gold and silver medals. 
 
 
• **Historical Facts:** 
 
• The first modern Olympics were held in **1896** in Athens, Greece, and featured no gold medals; winners received silver medals and olive branches. 
 
• The composition and design of medals are determined by the **host nation** and approved by the **International Olympic Committee**. 
 
• The **Tokyo 2020 Olympics** introduced medals made from recycled electronics to promote sustainability. 
 
 
• **Cultural Significance:** 
 
• Gold medals symbolize **victory, prestige, and excellence** and are often associated with great personal and national pride. 
 
• Winning a gold medal is considered the pinnacle of an athlete’s career and can inspire future generations to pursue sports. 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
 
• **Eligibility for Medals:** Athletes participate in various sports disciplines to compete for gold, silver, and bronze medals, which are awarded based on performance rankings. 
 
• **Medal Design:** The design of Olympic medals reflects the **cultural heritage** and identity of the host country. For example, the medals for the **Rio 2016 Olympics** featured elements of Brazilian culture. 
 
• **Medal Composition:** Gold medals contain a minimum of **92.5% silver** and are plated with at least **6 grams of gold**, ensuring durability and aesthetic appeal. 
 
• **Recognition and Rewards:** Many countries provide substantial rewards to Olympic medalists, such as **cash prizes, scholarships, or government honors**, to encourage sports excellence.

questions.question: Which author wrote the novel "Train to Pakistan"?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Khushwant Singh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Khushwant Singh**, a renowned Indian author and journalist, wrote the acclaimed novel **"Train to Pakistan."**
 
• The novel was published in **1956** and is considered one of the most significant literary works depicting the **Partition of India in 1947**.
 
• **"Train to Pakistan"** presents a vivid and realistic portrayal of the communal violence, displacement, and human suffering during the Partition.
 
• The story is set in the fictional village of **Mano Majra** located near the India-Pakistan border and captures the complex human emotions and relationships during this turbulent period.
 
• Khushwant Singh's writing style in this novel is characterized by its **straightforward narrative**, rich detailing, and an empathetic approach to the lives of ordinary people affected by the Partition.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Khushwant Singh:**
 
 
• Born on **2 February 1915** in Hadali, Punjab (now in Pakistan), Khushwant Singh is known for his **sharp wit**, satirical style, and profound commentary on socio-political issues.
 
• He worked as an editor for several prominent publications, including **The Illustrated Weekly of India** and **The Hindustan Times**.
 
• Singh was awarded the **Padma Bhushan** in **1974**, which he returned in protest against the Operation Blue Star in **1984**.
 
• Some of his other notable works include **"The Company of Women," "Delhi,"** and **"The History of Sikhs."**
 
 
 
• **Partition of India:**
 
 
• The Partition of India in **1947** led to the division of British India into two independent nations, **India and Pakistan**.
 
• It resulted in one of the largest migrations in history, with an estimated **15 million people displaced** and widespread communal violence.
 
• The Partition caused significant suffering, with a death toll ranging between **500,000 to 2 million**, as per various estimates.
 
 
 
• **The Novel's Themes:**
 
 
• **"Train to Pakistan"** explores themes such as **communal harmony**, the impact of political decisions on ordinary lives, and the atrocities of Partition.
 
• The novel delves into human emotions like **fear, love, betrayal, and survival** amidst chaos.
 
• It highlights the moral dilemmas faced by individuals and communities in times of crisis.
 
 
 
• **Other Options:**
 
 
• **Mulk Raj Anand:** Known for novels like **"Untouchable"** and **"Coolie,"** Anand focused on social realism and the plight of marginalized communities in India.
 
• **Arundhati Roy:** Famous for her Booker Prize-winning novel **"The God of Small Things."**
 
• **Vikram Seth:** Renowned for works like **"A Suitable Boy"**, which is one of the longest novels published in English.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The Partition of India was a result of the **Mountbatten Plan**, which divided the country along religious lines.
 
• It led to the creation of **West Pakistan** (modern-day Pakistan) and **East Pakistan** (now Bangladesh).
 
 
 
• **Literary Significance:**
 
 
• **"Train to Pakistan"** is considered a landmark in Indian literature for its realistic portrayal of historical events.
 
• It has been translated into several languages and adapted for stage performances and films.

questions.question: Which famous emperor patronized the development of Mathura art?

questions.question: How has the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) improved healthcare services?

options.text: By providing accurate diagnoses using data analysis
By eliminating the need for patient records

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By providing accurate diagnoses using data analysis**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• **Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Healthcare:** AI has been widely adopted in healthcare to enhance diagnostic accuracy, improve treatment planning, and optimize patient care. By analyzing large datasets of medical records and imaging, AI systems can identify patterns and anomalies that may not be immediately apparent to human doctors. 

• **Accurate Diagnoses:** AI-powered tools like machine learning algorithms and neural networks analyze patient data, including symptoms, medical history, and test results, to provide precise and early diagnoses of diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and cardiovascular disorders. 

• **Data Analysis:** AI systems process vast amounts of data in real-time. For example, IBM Watson Health uses AI to sift through medical literature and case studies to recommend the most effective treatments for specific conditions. 

• **Predictive Analytics:** AI enables predictive analytics, helping healthcare providers forecast disease outbreaks, patient deterioration, and hospital resource utilization. This contributes to proactive healthcare measures and better patient outcomes. 

• **Examples:** AI applications such as Google's DeepMind are used in diagnosing eye diseases, while AI-based radiology systems interpret X-rays and MRIs with high precision. This significantly reduces diagnostic errors and ensures timely treatment. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Applications of AI in Healthcare:** 
 

• **Medical Imaging:** AI algorithms are used to analyze CT scans, MRIs, and mammograms for detecting abnormalities like tumors or fractures. 

• **Drug Discovery:** AI accelerates the drug development process by identifying potential drug candidates and predicting their efficacy. 

• **Virtual Health Assistants:** Chatbots and virtual assistants powered by AI provide patients with health-related information, appointment scheduling, and symptom checking. 

• **Robotic Surgery:** AI-driven robotic systems like the da Vinci Surgical System assist surgeons in performing minimally invasive procedures with precision. 

• **Personalized Medicine:** AI tailors treatment plans based on an individual’s genetic makeup, lifestyle, and medical history for more effective outcomes. 
 
 

• **Global Impact:** 
 

• Countries like the **United States**, **United Kingdom**, and **India** are integrating AI into their healthcare systems to improve efficiency and accessibility. 

• AI adoption in healthcare is projected to grow at a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of **46.2%** between **2021** and **2027**, according to industry reports. 
 
 

• **Limitations:** 
 

• AI systems depend on the quality and quantity of data. Inaccurate or insufficient data can lead to errors in diagnosis or treatment recommendations. 

• Ethical concerns, such as patient data privacy and the potential for bias in AI algorithms, must be addressed to ensure fair and equitable healthcare delivery. 
 
 

• **AI vs. Human Expertise:** While AI enhances decision-making, it does not replace doctors. Human oversight remains essential for interpreting AI-generated insights and providing compassionate patient care.

• **Incorrect Options Explained:** 
 

• **Option 1 (By replacing all doctors):** AI complements rather than replaces healthcare professionals. Human expertise is irreplaceable in aspects like empathy, ethical decision-making, and patient interaction. 

• **Option 2 (By reducing hospital infrastructure):** AI focuses on enhancing processes and patient care rather than reducing physical infrastructure. 

• **Option 4 (By eliminating the need for patient records):** On the contrary, AI relies heavily on electronic health records (EHRs) for data analysis and diagnosis. 
 
 

• **Real-World Examples:** 
 

• **DeepMind:** Used in the UK’s National Health Service (NHS) to predict kidney failure risks. 

• **PathAI:** Assists pathologists in diagnosing diseases accurately through AI-powered tools. 
 
 

• **Future Potential:** AI is expected to play a larger role in telemedicine, mental health support, and global healthcare accessibility in the coming years.
